q: A bank's account and payment services are used only by its own mobile app; no outside party can build on them. A colleague calls this a platform. Do you agree?
a: Only partly. It fits the engineering definition, a set of services that applications are built and run on, but not the business one: no outside parties build complementary products through its interfaces, so it has no ecosystem yet. The lecture expects both internal consumption and external complements. To get there the bank would need published, extensible interfaces that partners can build against.

q: A company hosts its reusable services on a shared cluster but leaves service discovery, resource coordination and usage reporting to each application team. What is missing compared with the lecture's definition of a modern platform, and why does it matter?
a: A modern platform is both an application architecture and the infrastructure that hosts it, so it must solve discovery, resource coordination, orchestration and usage reporting itself. Left to each team, these concerns get solved differently and repeatedly, and the company is sharing components rather than offering a platform. Taking them on makes the platform team responsible for infrastructure, which is the work platform engineering exists to do.

q: A payments API is PCI-compliant and encrypts every transaction, but partners need three weeks of contracts and manual key exchange before their first test call, and there is no sandbox. Which platform characteristic is weakest, and what would you change?
a: **Quick to start using** is weakest: the on-ramp is slow and costly, which discourages producers and consumers from joining. Add quick-start guides, code samples, self-service test credentials and a test card suite, as Google Pay does. Security and compliance should stay the default, so the sandbox must not expose real card data.

q: A platform team wants to replace its internal database and messaging stack. Dozens of partner apps call its published APIs. Which platform benefit lets the team do this without a partner release, and what would break it?
a: The separation of intra-platform from inter-platform change: stable interfaces let the inside evolve at its own pace without overly impacting the outside. It breaks if the change leaks through the interface, for example by altering response fields or meanings. Then the team needs a new API version and a migration period for partners.

q: A platform logs every transaction, but nobody analyses the logs and its service catalogue has not changed in two years. Which characteristic is it failing, and why is collecting data not enough?
a: It is failing **stays relevant and data-driven**. That characteristic needs a feedback loop, data collected and then analysed to improve the services, as with Google Pay's analysis of spending or ML fraud detection. Logs nobody reads support no decisions, so the platform drifts away from what its users need.

q: Your team adopts a toolkit that supplies abstract classes, dictates how the application is structured and calls your code at points it defines. A teammate calls it a library. Do you agree?
a: No, it is a framework: a predefined skeleton that imposes a way of architecting the application and supports certain design patterns. A library is code you call from your own application at points you choose. The distinction matters because a framework shapes the whole design, so replacing it later costs far more than swapping a library.

q: An internal team announces 'we are building a platform', but its deliverable is a downloadable code skeleton that each app team installs and runs on its own servers. Is that a platform?
a: No, it is a framework, which can be part of a platform but is not one. A platform is the environment software runs in: it provides hosted services and reusable components accessed by APIs, lets applications extend features by consuming and exposing services, and collects data for analytics. To become a platform the team would need to host and operate shared services, not just distribute code.

q: A company's developers wait several days for an ops ticket to be approved before they get a test database. Which pain point is this, and what is the platform engineering answer?
a: It is ticket ops: no self-service, so developers queue on operations for routine provisioning. Platform engineering replaces the ticket with a self-service capability, a portal, CLI or workload spec that provisions the database through an automated, standardised workflow. The platform team must then own and maintain that automation as a product.

q: A CTO says: 'We already have a DevOps culture and an SRE team, so a platform team would be redundant.' Do you agree?
a: No. The lecture presents them as complementary: DevOps is culture and CI/CD with shared responsibility, and SRE applies software engineering to reliability through SLOs, error budgets and toil reduction. Neither builds an internal developer platform that treats developers as customers and offers self-service golden paths. If the organisation has only a few teams and services, though, the scale problem a platform team solves may not exist yet.

q: Thirty application teams each maintain their own copied-and-edited pipeline scripts and infrastructure code. Which pain points does this show, and what would a platform offer?
a: It shows no standardisation, lack of automation through repeated manual work, and developer cognitive overload, three of the top drivers in the survey. A platform would provide a golden path: a supported, opinionated pipeline and provisioning route that every team can reuse. The cost is less freedom for teams with unusual needs, so the platform team has to gather feedback and evolve the path.

q: Six months after launch, a platform team wants to prove ROI and proposes reporting the number of portal logins per week. Does that metric show the platform's value?
a: No. Logins measure activity, not delivery performance, and they can rise simply because teams are forced onto the portal. Compare the DORA metrics (deployment frequency, lead time, MTTR, change failure rate) against the baseline measured before launch, together with developer NPS. Logins are useful only as a secondary adoption signal.

q: After a platform launch, deployment frequency rises but change failure rate also rises. Has the platform clearly improved delivery?
a: No. Delivery is faster but less reliable, so the evidence is mixed. Check lead time and MTTR as well, and look at whether the golden path is missing tests or guardrails that teams used to apply by hand. Developer feedback shows whether the automation reduces or just moves the effort.

q: In a GitOps setup, an engineer fixes a production configuration by editing the cluster directly. What happens next, and what should they have done?
a: Git is the single source of truth, so the CD tool keeps syncing the cluster to Git and will overwrite the manual change, or leave it as unrecorded drift. The change should go through a pull request, so it is reviewed, versioned and reproducible. GitOps trades the speed of a direct edit for auditability and repeatability.

q: Developers on your platform currently write raw cluster manifests and infrastructure code for every service. A teammate proposes a workload spec in the developer control plane with an orchestrator behind it. What does this buy, and what does it cost?
a: Developers would declare **what** a workload needs, such as a database or a port, without infrastructure knowledge, and the orchestrator would decide **how** by generating app and infrastructure configs as a resource graph on each deployment. That lowers cognitive load and keeps standards and security consistent across teams. The cost is that the platform team must build and maintain the orchestrator rules, and developers lose direct control of details.

q: A security lead proposes one security scan as the final stage before production. Where does the reference architecture put security, and why does that matter?
a: Security is a cross-cutting plane, embedded everywhere: secrets management, identity, access control, policies and compliance apply to every plane, not just the last step. A single final gate finds problems late and leaves secrets and access in earlier stages unmanaged. Embedding it costs more platform work up front but makes the secure path the default.

q: A developer's workload spec is accepted, but the service fails in staging because no database exists there. Using the planes, where would you look first?
a: The orchestrator in the integration and delivery plane turns the spec into a resource graph for each environment, and the resource plane provisions what that graph asks for. So check whether the staging resource graph includes the database and whether provisioning ran. The observability plane should give logs from every plane, which shows why cross-cutting monitoring matters.

q: A data science team wants to train and deploy models through the existing IDP. What does the reference model add for them, and why is the resource plane alone not enough?
a: It adds the data and model management plane: feature engineering, experiment tracking, metadata, lineage and a model registry, covering the ML lifecycle up to production governance. The resource plane can supply GPU nodes, but it does not track which data and experiment produced which model. Without that plane the platform can run ML workloads but cannot govern them.

q: A platform team's first deliverable is a polished developer portal, while provisioning behind it is still done by ticket. Do you support the plan?
a: No. The lecture's principle is backend before portal: a portal is only an interface, and with ticket-driven provisioning behind it nothing self-service happens. Build the automation for the top pain first, typically CI/CD and IaC, golden paths and an orchestrator, then put a portal or CLI on top. A portal can come early only as a thin front for automation that already works.

q: A security lead wants every developer to run three extra scanning tools by hand before each merge. Is this shifting left or shifting down, and what would you suggest?
a: It is shifting left: it moves checks earlier but dumps the toil on developers. Shifting down would embed the scans in the platform as automated guardrails and secure defaults on the golden path, so the safe route is also the easiest. The checks can still run early; what changes is who does the work.

q: A platform team plans an 18-month build covering every plane before any application team uses it. What would you change?
a: Start with a minimum viable platform that solves the most costly pain, then expand. A long build with no users delays value and gets no feedback, so the team may build the wrong things, against the 'treat it as a product' principle. Measure from day one so each step's impact is visible.

q: A maturity survey shows most organisations stuck at 'Operational', with measurement the weakest dimension. Your new platform team has no baseline numbers. What do you do first, and why?
a: Document the current cost of the pain, such as ticket wait times, lead time and failure rates, before building anything. A platform is a product that must prove ROI, and without a baseline no later DORA or NPS figure can show improvement. It is cheap to do at the start and almost impossible to reconstruct later.

q: A video site runs separate marketing budgets for creators and for viewers, treating them as two markets. What does 'think roles not markets' suggest instead?
a: Users can play both roles, and viewers can become creators. The magnet strategy converts consumers into producers over time, which saves marketing spend and scales production of seeds. So invest in lowering the barrier to producing, such as simple upload tools, rather than buying two separate audiences.

q: A tutoring marketplace has plenty of registered tutors, but students complain that matches are poor and some tutors are low quality. Which platform component is weak, and what would you build?
a: The matchmaker, not the magnet: supply exists, but matching and curation fail. Improve matching accuracy to cut false positives, curate tutors using ratings and reviews, add trust mechanisms, and apply ML to matching. In engineering terms that means curation components and matching algorithms.

q: A furniture maker sells only its own products through its web shop and calls itself a platform because the shop has a public API. Is this a linear or a network business?
a: Linear: its focus is the process of production, assembly and distribution of its own goods. A network business focuses on enabling interactions between independent producers and consumers, and the lecture stresses that technology is only an enabler, so an API alone does not make a platform. It would move towards a network model if other makers could list and sell through it.

q: A start-up wants to launch professional networking, messaging, job listings and content publishing all at once. What does the LinkedIn example advise?
a: Build one interaction at a time. LinkedIn started with professional-to-professional connections, then added discussions, recruiters and job seekers, and later thought-leader content, each one building adoption before monetisation. Launching everything at once spreads the magnet thin, with too few producers for any single interaction.

q: Partners praise a platform's matching algorithm but say its SDK is confusing and integration takes weeks. Which platform aspect is weak, and which engineering concerns does it map to?
a: The toolbox: the tools producers and consumers use to interact. In engineering terms that is service usability design, SDK and API design, and integration with other services. A strong matchmaker cannot make up for a toolbox that keeps partners from joining.

q: Hundreds of third-party apps now depend on a platform's interfaces. A product manager proposes putting all of this quarter's effort into new features and deferring availability and security work. Do you agree?
a: Mostly no. Architecting for the ecosystem means availability, security and scalability, because an outage or breach now hits every complement built on the platform, not just one app. Features still matter for growth, so the answer depends on whether current availability and security already meet partners' needs.

q: A platform plans to add a new kind of interaction every quarter, as the sample paper's ecosystem-growth question describes. Which engineering aspect must the design support, and what goes wrong without it?
a: Scaling the platform business needs modular, extensible components and an agile architecture. Each new interaction should plug in as new services that reuse existing domain entities and interfaces. Without that, every addition means changing the core, so each release slows down and risks breaking existing interactions.

q: A food-delivery company wants to open its ordering, delivery-tracking and payment capabilities to independent restaurants and couriers. (a) Identify the seed, producers, consumers and core interaction. (b) The CEO wants to launch restaurant booking, grocery delivery and a courier marketplace in the same release. Advise. (c) Give two engineering concerns that follow from opening the APIs to outside parties.
a: (a) Seed: a menu item or order; producers: restaurants and couriers; consumers: diners; interaction: browse, order, match a courier, deliver, pay. (b) Build one interaction at a time, as LinkedIn did: get food ordering adopted and growing producers through the magnet before adding new interactions, and design modular, extensible components so later ones plug in. (c) The toolbox needs usable APIs and SDKs, and because many outside parties now depend on the platform it must be architected for availability, security and scalability. The trade-off is slower initial scope in exchange for a stable core.

q: A company with 40 application teams has a five-day ticket wait for databases, each team maintains its own pipeline scripts, and leadership wants evidence of value within six months. Propose the first steps of an IDP, the measures you would use, and one thing you would deliberately not build first.
a: First document the cost of the pain (ticket wait, lead time, failure rates) as a baseline. Define a minimum viable platform aimed at the top pain: automated database provisioning through IaC and a shared CI/CD golden path, with an orchestrator or pipeline behind it. Measure DORA metrics and developer NPS against the baseline, and expand scope only where they improve. Do not start with a full developer portal: backend comes before portal, and a portal over ticket-driven provisioning would show nothing in six months.

q: On an IDP, developers submit workload specs. Staging deployments work, but production sometimes gets a different database size and nobody can explain why. Using the reference architecture and GitOps, diagnose where to look and what to change.
a: The orchestrator in the integration and delivery plane generates environment-specific configuration as a resource graph, so compare the production and staging graphs and the rules that produce them. Check whether production state was changed outside Git: with GitOps, Git should be the single source of truth and every infra change should go through a reviewed PR. Fix by moving environment differences into versioned config and letting CD sync from Git. The observability plane should record what was deployed, so the next difference is visible without detective work.

q: An organisation with 300 developers has a DevOps culture and an SRE team that owns SLOs and error budgets, but onboarding a new service still takes three weeks. The CIO asks whether to grow the SRE team or create a platform team. Advise, and say what would change your answer.
a: Create a platform team. The symptom is slow onboarding and missing self-service, which are platform engineering's concerns: golden paths, standardised provisioning and lower cognitive load, with developers treated as customers. SRE keeps owning reliability, and the platform can make SLO monitoring a default for every new service. If the main problem were frequent outages or missed SLOs instead of slow onboarding, growing SRE would be the better answer.

q: A regulated firm requires secret scanning, dependency checks and policy checks for every service. Option A gives each team a checklist to run before release. Option B builds the checks into the platform's golden path. Choose one and give the trade-off.
a: Choose B, shifting down. Embedding the checks as automated guardrails and secure defaults removes repeated manual toil, applies the rules consistently, and makes the compliant path the easiest one, which fits the security plane being cross-cutting. Option A is shifting left: checks happen early, but every team carries the work and compliance depends on each team's discipline. B costs platform investment up front, and teams that leave the golden path still need a way to show compliance.

q: A bank's architecture group plans to give its teams (a) a shared code skeleton with abstract classes, (b) a utility code package for date and currency handling, and (c) a hosted environment exposing identity and payment services through APIs, which partners may also use. Classify each, and explain which one creates an ecosystem and what that obliges the bank to do.
a: (a) is a framework: teams use it and it dictates structure. (b) is a library: teams call it where they choose. (c) is a platform: hosted, accessed by APIs, and extensible by outside parties. Only (c) creates an ecosystem, because partners can build complementary products through its interfaces. That obliges the bank to keep those interfaces stable so internal change does not break partners, and to architect for availability, security and scalability.

q: The Purchase client and the Purchase service both need the same Order entity classes, and the Purchase and Delivery services both need customer details. Which kind of reusable asset fits each need?
a: Share the Order entities through a **shared library** used by the Purchase client and service: that is reuse of classes at a small scale. Get customer details from a **Customer service** that Purchase and Delivery both call, because that is reuse of a business capability across features. The library ties client and service releases together, and the service adds a remote call, so each choice has a cost.

q: A platform team must build ten new services quickly, all with the same web conventions, configuration and request handling. Should it reuse a service, a framework or a shared library?
a: A framework, such as Spring Boot in the lecture: frameworks are reused to build many clients and services and give them a common structure and behaviour. A service provides a capability at runtime, not a way to build services, and a library supplies classes without imposing the overall structure. The catch is that a good framework is expensive to design, so it pays off only when many services will use it.

q: A proposed Customer service can scale only when the Order service scales with it, because the two share an in-process session cache. Which reusable-service characteristic does this break, and what would you change?
a: It breaks horizontal scalability without depending on other services, and loose coupling. Give each service its own state and talk through its interface or messages, which the lecture calls the loosest coupling. The cost is some duplicated data and having to accept eventual consistency between the two.

q: A team used DDD to find well-bounded services, but each release still takes a week of manual packaging and deployment. A manager blames the domain design. Do you agree?
a: Mostly no. DDD produces designs that satisfy the IDEALS principles except **Deployability**, which comes from DevOps automation of packaging and deployment, so the fix is pipelines, not boundaries. The manager would have a point only if the boundaries force several services to be released in lockstep, because that is a coupling problem in the design.

q: In a code review, a domain entity class imports the database driver and saves itself. Which onion-architecture rule does this break, and why does it matter for a reusable service?
a: Dependencies must point toward the centre: inner layers define interfaces and outer layers implement them, so the application core compiles and runs without infrastructure. Define a repository interface in the core and implement it in the outer layer. The core can then be tested and reused with a different store, at the cost of one more interface and adapter.

q: While modelling a service with DDD, a team adds RetryPolicy and HttpClientWrapper classes to the domain model. Should these be there?
a: No. DDD focuses squarely on domain objects and leaves out non-domain concerns, while OOAD would add design and framework objects in later stages. Retry and HTTP handling still need designing, but in the outer layers around the domain model. Mixing them in blurs the ubiquitous language and ties the core to infrastructure.

q: You receive a 60-entity domain model for a new platform and two weeks to propose services. Do you start by designing aggregates or by drawing bounded contexts?
a: Bounded contexts first. Strategic design is coarse-grained: it divides the domain into contexts, sets each one's ubiquitous language and classifies core and subdomains. Aggregates are tactical, fine-grained clusters inside one context, so designing them first risks clusters that cut across what should be separate contexts. Revisit the context boundaries once aggregate design shows where invariants really sit.

q: When a backlog item is committed to a sprint, the resource-management context must update team availability. A teammate proposes that resource management reads the core context's tables directly. What would you use instead, and why?
a: Have the core publish a domain event such as BacklogItemCommitted and let resource management react to it in its own transaction. Each context keeps its own schema and model, so the core can change its tables without breaking a consumer. The price is eventual consistency: availability is updated shortly after the commit, not in the same transaction.

q: An e-commerce firm wins business through its pricing and recommendation engine; identity, billing and notifications look like everyone else's. Which is the core domain, and what does that classification change in your design?
a: Pricing and recommendation is the core domain: it is the context critical to the business. Identity, billing and notifications are supporting or generic subdomains. Classifying them tells you where the model needs the most refinement, and which generic contexts are candidates to split out and reuse across systems.

q: Underwriting, Claims and Inspections all use the word 'Policy'. An architect proposes one canonical Policy entity shared by all three teams. Do you agree?
a: No. Inside each bounded context, Policy has a specific meaning and does specific things, so a single shared entity has to carry every context's attributes and rules and becomes coupled to all three teams. DDD segregates them into separate models with their own ubiquitous language and translates at the boundaries. The cost is that business and technical people must agree explicitly on what Policy means in each context.

q: Two teams share one repository and one database schema for the Claims bounded context, and both change its interfaces. What problems would you expect, and what does the lecture prescribe?
a: Expect conflicting changes to the model and interfaces, unclear ownership, and schema changes from one team breaking the other. The lecture prescribes one team per bounded context (a team may own several), a separate repository with source, acceptance and unit tests together, a separate schema, and interfaces defined by the owning team. If the context is too big for one team, the boundary itself is probably wrong.

q: Every new feature adds entities to one shared domain model. The test suite now takes hours and teams disagree about what 'Account' means. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix.
a: It is a Big Ball of Mud: tangled models, blurred language and no explicit boundaries. Split the entities by functional cohesion into bounded contexts, each with one ubiquitous language, so 'Account' can mean different things in different contexts. Each context gets a smaller test set and can become the boundary for a service, repository, schema and team. The split costs integration work between contexts that used to share objects.

q: A group of developers tries to find bounded contexts from the existing database schema alone, without domain experts. What is the risk?
a: The schema reflects the current, possibly tangled, model, so it tends to reproduce the Big Ball of Mud rather than the business's own boundaries. The lecture requires domain experts, whose mental model drives entity extraction, and developers who engage with business aspects instead of being consumed by technology. The schema is useful evidence, but the boundaries should come from iterating on a combined model with the experts.

q: From the scenario 'the product owner commits a backlog item to a sprint only if it is scheduled for release and a quorum of team members approved', a junior developer makes Quorum an entity. Do you agree?
a: Probably not. Nouns are candidate entities, but the lecture warns that some nouns are properties of an entity, and here quorum approval is a pre-condition on the commitment. Model it as part of the commitment rule. It would become an entity only if individual approvals must be tracked and changed over time.

q: A team records its ubiquitous language as a glossary document kept apart from the code and tests. What does the lecture's approach add?
a: Restate the concrete scenarios as executable Given/When/Then specifications that serve as acceptance tests. The language then stays tied to verifiable behaviour, such as the backlog item becoming committed and the BacklogItemCommitted event being created. A separate glossary drifts from the code without anyone noticing.

q: In the Scrum tool split, Discussion appears in both the core context and the collaboration context. A reviewer flags it as duplication to remove. How do you respond?
a: It is not a defect. Each bounded context has its own ubiquitous language and model, so the same name can mean and do different things in each. Merging them would recreate a shared model that couples the core to collaboration features. What is needed is an explicit mapping between them wherever the two contexts interact.

q: Another product line also needs tenant billing with accounts and payments, which the Scrum tool already has in its billing context. What does the lecture's procedure suggest?
a: Split a bounded context further if the resulting contexts are more reusable across systems. Keep billing as a separate generic subdomain with no dependency on project-management concepts, so the other product can reuse it. The billing context then needs a stable interface and an owner who serves both consumers.

q: A teammate proposes merging MaidOrderManager and MaidLoanManager into a single ServiceOrderManager, because both have plans, usages and bills. Do you agree?
a: No. Customer orders and agency-to-agency loans are different business functions with different parties and plans (OnceAFortnight, OnceAWeek and TwiceAWeek for customers; Weekly and Monthly for loans), so each has its own ubiquitous language: MaidUsage and MaidUsagePlan against MaidLoanUsage and MaidLoanPlan. A merged context would change for two unrelated reasons and blur those terms. The cost of keeping them apart is some parallel structure.

q: Maid2Order adds a new digital-wallet payment method. Using the lecture's sample solution, which contexts change, and which should not?
a: Only PaymentManager: add a new ElectronicPayment specialisation alongside BankTransfer, PayNow and CreditCardPayment, still producing a Receipt. BillingManager, MaidOrderManager and MaidLoanManager do not change, because they deal with bills and a payment simply settles a Bill. If they did need to change, that would show the payment details had leaked across the boundary.

q: A teammate proposes moving MaidUsageBill, MaidLoanBill and PlatformMonthlyBill into BillingManager so that every bill type lives in one place. Do you agree?
a: No. Each specific bill belongs to the context whose business activity produces it, and BillingManager holds only the common Bill they lead to. Pulling the specific types in would make BillingManager depend on ordering, loan and platform-usage rules, so it would change whenever they do and could not be reused elsewhere. The cost of the lecture's design is a translation from each specific bill to Bill at the boundary.

q: In the sample solution, Customer in CustomerManager holds only the customer's particulars. Where should the customer's current usage plan live, and why?
a: In MaidOrderManager, as a MaidUsage under a MaidUsagePlan that refers to the customer. Ordering is that context's responsibility, so CustomerManager stays small and reusable. The two contexts are linked by a reference, not a shared object, which means a screen showing both needs data from two services.

q: A platform's web, mobile, backend and partner services are built by different teams, each with its own way of calling the others and handling errors. What problem does this create, and what does the lecture recommend?
a: Interactions are inconsistent, so every pair of systems needs custom integration, and the same behaviour is rebuilt many times. The lecture says the platform provider should use frameworks to standardise common behaviours and the interactions between services and clients. The cost is the design effort of the framework and less freedom for teams with unusual needs.

q: A ministry plans for each agency to build its own citizen-facing services and infrastructure, since each serves a different group. Using the SGTS case, argue against this, and say what is given up.
a: Separate stacks duplicate effort, give citizens an inconsistent experience and make it hard to exchange data across agencies. SGTS puts a common platform of tools and services on common infrastructure, so agencies build faster, with a more secure, consistent and connected experience and easier data exchange for policy insights. Agencies give up some freedom and depend on the central platform's roadmap and availability.

q: Users of your framework fall into two groups: beginners who want one call to send a payment, and experts who need control over retries and the wire format. How do you serve both?
a: Use a layered architecture: a lower layer with rich, low-level types exposes all the power, and a higher layer wraps it in convenient calls for the common case. That makes simple things simple and complex things possible, which a single-layer API cannot do. The cost is designing and keeping two consistent layers.

q: A three-person team is building a framework for its own applications; a 20-person team is building one for external partners. Which framework-design process model fits each?
a: The small team fits the model in which designers alternate between building applications on the framework and consolidating good extensions, provided they can budget effort for revision. The larger group targeting external users fits the more popular model: designers design and test, application builders extend it and give feedback, and designers revise. That model only works if designers have enough time set aside for the revisions.

q: Partners are pressing for a framework, and the team wants to publish v1 to all of them after one internal application has used it. Advise.
a: Hold back: one application is unlikely to be representative, and publishing while the design is still changing means unstable interfaces ripple into every partner's code. Validate it through a few small pilot projects and release once suggestions for improvement become rare. Partners wait longer but avoid painful rework, and 'you can always add, you cannot ever remove' argues against shipping half-finished parts just to have them.

q: A design review finds that one module of the framework names things and handles errors differently from the rest. Why is this a concern, and when could it be justified?
a: Consistency across the framework promotes productivity and lets knowledge transfer from one part to another, and a deviation signals that the part is genuinely different. An accidental inconsistency sends that signal falsely and confuses users. It is justified only when the module really has a unique consideration, and then the difference should be deliberate and documented.

q: To obey DRY, a teammate proposes a common-domain library of Customer, Order and Payment classes used by all 12 services. Do you agree?
a: No. A shared domain library couples every service to it: one change forces coordinated changes and redeployments across all 12, which undermines independent release and blurs bounded contexts. The lecture's rule is not to violate DRY within a service but to be relaxed about DRY across services. The price is some duplicated code, which is cheaper than lockstep releases.

q: Your platform will publish client libraries for its APIs. Option A: the API team writes a smart client that handles discovery, failures and logging, and all callers must use it. Option B: thin SDKs maintained separately, with callers choosing when to upgrade. Choose.
a: Option B for a platform with varied consumers. Like the AWS SDKs, it keeps clients loosely coupled to the server and lets them upgrade on their own schedule. Option A, the Netflix style, gets clients running quickly and reliably but couples them tightly, invites server logic into the client, and limits technology choices if it is mandated. A could suit a single organisation on one technology stack that values uniform resilience.

q: After a fix to a shared library, three services that did not need the fix have to be rebuilt and redeployed, and a Python client cannot use the library at all. Which drawbacks are these, and what would reduce them?
a: A new library version cannot be deployed without redeploying the whole process, and the library is language-specific, so technology heterogeneity is lost. Shared communication code is a coupling point, much like regenerated RMI stubs. Reduce it by not sharing code across service boundaries, separating transport-protocol code from service-specific code, and letting clients decide when to upgrade.

q: The team that owns the Order service also writes its client library, and order-validation rules have started to appear in the library. What is the risk?
a: Server logic is creeping into the client library, which the lecture says is especially likely when the same team owns both. The server's cohesion breaks down, and fixing a rule now means changing and rolling out many clients instead of one service. Keep the rules in the service and limit the library to making calls convenient.

q: A ride-hailing platform's NotificationService defines every notification type itself, including TripAssigned, FareReceipt, DriverPayoutReady and PromoOffer, each with content specific to another service's responsibility. The company wants to reuse it in its new food-delivery platform without major adaptation. Identify the most likely cause of poor reusability, propose a countermeasure by revising the domain model, and give its main drawback.
a: Cause: the service is not cohesive or single-minded. It holds knowledge that belongs to the Trip, Payment, Payout and Marketing contexts, so it is coupled to this platform's domain. Countermeasure: make it a generic subdomain that models only generic concepts, such as a notification with recipient, channel, template and delivery status, and move each specific notification's content into the context that owns the event, which requests sending through a published interface or by publishing domain events. Drawback: every owning service now has to compose its own notifications, and there is more integration and some repeated formatting code across services.

q: A logistics company has one shared model in which 'Shipment' means a customer order in Sales, a truck load in Dispatch and a customs declaration in Compliance. One team of 25 owns the code and a single database. Propose a restructuring of contexts, teams, repositories and data, and name one new problem it creates.
a: Split into Sales, Dispatch and Compliance bounded contexts, each with its own ubiquitous language, so 'Shipment' gets a precise meaning in each, for example Order, Load and Declaration, or the same name with separate models. Give each context one owning team, its own repository with code and acceptance and unit tests, its own schema and interfaces defined by that team. Integrate through explicit interfaces or domain events, not shared tables. New problem: a change that spans contexts now needs coordination and translation between models, with eventual consistency instead of one local transaction.

q: In the Scrum tool, the product owner commits a backlog item to a sprint; it must already be scheduled for release, a quorum must approve, and if it is in another sprint it must be uncommitted first. Write the Given/When/Then specification, identify the aggregate or aggregates involved, and say how both sprints learn about the change.
a: Given a backlog item scheduled for release, its product owner, a target sprint and quorum approval; When the product owner commits it to the sprint; Then it is committed to the sprint and a BacklogItemCommitted event is created. The commitment rule sits with the backlog item, the aggregate whose invariant it is, and the sprint is referenced rather than changed in the same transaction. The previous sprint and the new sprint learn of it by reacting to the domain event, which keeps each transaction small but makes their views eventually consistent. The scenario wording also becomes part of the context's ubiquitous language and doubles as an acceptance test.

q: Maid2Order adds corporate customers: a company subscribes to maid services for several offices and wants one monthly invoice. Using the lecture's seven-context solution, place the new concepts, justify each placement, and name one context that should not change.
a: The corporate customer and its offices belong in CustomerManager as a kind of Customer, because that context holds the party's particulars. The per-office services stay in MaidOrderManager as MaidUsage under usage plans, because ordering rules live there. The single monthly invoice belongs in BillingManager, whose common Bill can consolidate the usage bills. PaymentManager should not change, since it simply settles a Bill. If corporate contracts turn out to have very different rules, a separate context may be justified, at the cost of more integration.

q: A platform's 15 services all need (a) customer-profile lookups, (b) the same request logging, tracing and configuration conventions, and (c) a Money value class. Choose service, framework or shared library for each, and state the risk of each choice.
a: (a) A Customer service: reuse of a business capability, scaled and released independently; the risk is remote-call latency and failures, so callers need timeouts. (b) A framework, which standardises common behaviour for building many services; the risk is that it is expensive to design well and ties services to its release cycle. (c) A shared library for a small, stable value class; the risk is coupling and language lock-in, so share only stable technical types and keep domain models within each service.

q: A four-person platform team must deliver an integration framework for 30 partner companies in nine months. Propose the design process and the qualities you would check, and name the pitfall you fear most.
a: Analyse example integrations from several representative partners, design scenario-first from sample client code, and build a whitebox version for them. Pilot it with two or three partners, collect feedback (the external-user process model), make the framework more blackbox, and release widely only when suggestions become rare. Check simplicity, low barrier of entry, self-documenting names, a layered design for power users, consistency, testability and backward compatibility. The biggest pitfall is premature release under schedule pressure with unrepresentative examples, since unstable interfaces would then ripple into 30 partners' code.

q: A bank exposes each table of its core system as its own API and calls the job done. Six months later almost nobody uses them. Diagnose the problem.
a: It is inside-out design: the APIs expose existing resources rather than what consumers need, so developers find them hard to use or not useful. An outside-in strategy starts from the needs of developers and end users, launches an MVP, and measures success by adoption and business impact through usage analytics. The bank should treat the APIs as a product with an owner who iterates on that feedback.

q: An API team is disbanded the week after launch because 'the project is delivered'. What goes wrong over the next year?
a: Nobody acts on usage analytics or developer feedback, so the API stops improving. Versions, documentation and endpoint stability are no longer managed, so consumers meet breaking changes and stale docs. The lecture's point is that APIs should be managed as products, not projects: a product owner keeps a backlog from feedback and matures the API through iterations.

q: A single endpoint, /process-customer, creates a customer, opens an account and sends a welcome pack in one call. A partner only needs to create customers. Critique the design.
a: It breaks the granularity principles: one API with several responsibilities, which forces the partner to depend on behaviour it does not use, against single responsibility and interface segregation. Design at the lowest practical level, with separate customer and account resources, so consumers can combine them in different ways. Clients that need all three steps now make more calls, which a composite at the gateway can hide if needed.

q: A platform publishes its API with only a Java SDK and a custom binary protocol. Which design principle does this break, and what would you change?
a: Ubiquitous standards: develop APIs on well-accepted standards and make no assumptions about the consumer's technology. A custom protocol with one SDK excludes consumers on other stacks and slows adoption. Expose a standard protocol such as HTTP with JSON and maintain SDKs for several technologies; the cost is more SDKs to maintain.

q: An API keeps each user's session in the memory of the instance that served the login, so the load balancer uses sticky sessions. Traffic triples during a sale and one instance crashes. What goes wrong, and what does REST's stateless constraint suggest?
a: Users pinned to the crashed instance lose their sessions, and load cannot be spread evenly because requests must return to their own instance. With statelessness the client holds the application state and each request carries its own context, so any instance can serve any request and you scale by adding instances, with no server-side session synchronisation. Persistent resource data still needs a shared store.

q: An API runs on eight instances, each with an in-process cache of product prices. Users see different prices depending on which instance answers. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix.
a: Each in-process cache is local to its instance, so updates reach the caches at different times. A distributed cache is consistent across requests to multiple servers and survives restarts and deployments. It is slower than local memory and is another service to run, and it still needs a policy for invalidating stale entries.

q: Pick an API style for (a) in-app chat, (b) telling a partner system the moment a file upload completes, and (c) a mobile dashboard whose data needs vary by screen. Justify each choice.
a: (a) WebSocket, for continuous two-way real-time messages. (b) A webhook, an event notification that calls the partner when the upload happens, so the partner does not have to poll. (c) GraphQL, so each screen asks for exactly the fields it needs in one request. These match the lecture's typical uses, and a REST API could still serve (c) if HTTP caching matters more than flexible queries.

q: A reviewer says your API is not RESTful because the server never sends scripts for the client to run. Do you agree?
a: No. Code on demand is the one REST constraint that is not strictly required: it lets the server extend a client by sending code, which reduces what the client must pre-implement. The required constraints are client-server, stateless, uniform interface, layered system and caching, so review the API against those instead.

q: Critique this orders API and rewrite it: POST /createOrder; GET /orders/delete?id=9; PUT /orders with the new order in the body; GET /getCustomers?customer-id=7&orders-id=9; GET /products/sort/price/page/2.
a: Resources should be plural nouns with no verbs, so use POST /orders to create (201). GET must be safe, so deletion becomes DELETE /orders/9. PUT updates a known resource, so use PUT /orders/9 or PATCH /orders/9. Use path variables for identity and relationships, GET /customers/7/orders/9, and query parameters only to shape results: GET /products?sort=price&page=2&limit=50.

q: A mobile client times out on POST /payments and retries. How do you make sure the customer is not charged twice?
a: Generate one idempotency key for the intended payment and send the same key on every retry. The server records the key with the outcome and, on a repeat, returns the recorded result without charging again. Generating a fresh key per attempt defeats the protection, and the server must keep keys long enough to cover the retry window.

q: A client times out on DELETE /orders/9, retries, and gets 404. A developer fears the retry did harm. Did it?
a: No. DELETE is idempotent: idempotency concerns server state, and after one or several calls the order is gone either way. Only the response differs, typically 204 then 404, so the client should treat a 404 on a retried delete as 'already deleted'.

q: A cart API offers PATCH /carts/5/items/3 with either {"quantity": 5} or {"increment": 1}. The client library retries PATCH automatically on timeout. Is that safe?
a: Only for the first form. Setting quantity to 5 leaves the same state however often it repeats, but incrementing by 1 adds another item on every retry. PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent, so either disable automatic retries for the increment or protect it with an idempotency key.

q: An API returns 200 with the body {"error": "customer not found"} for unknown customers, and 500 when the client sends malformed JSON. What is wrong, and what should it return?
a: Return 404 for the missing customer and 400 for the malformed request. Status codes tell the developer who behaved wrongly: 4xx means the client did, 5xx means the API did. As built, clients cannot handle errors from the status code, and monitoring raises server alarms for client mistakes while missing real failures.

q: A clerk with a valid token calls DELETE /accounts/7, which only managers may do, and the API returns 401. Is that the right code?
a: No, it should be 403: the credentials were accepted, but the caller lacks permission for this resource. A 401 tells the client its credentials are missing or not recognised, so the client may try to log in again, which cannot help. Clear codes improve developer experience and make the API easier to adopt.

q: Since this morning's release, 2% of requests return 500. A developer proposes changing code directly on a production server to test a theory. How do you respond?
a: Don't: blind changes in production are the lecture's 'big mistake', because they can widen the outage and leave no audit trail. Correlate logs, metrics and traces to find the failing path, compare against what the release changed, and reproduce safely. If the release is the cause, roll back, then ship a verified fix through the normal pipeline.

q: A downstream dependency is down for planned maintenance for ten minutes. Should your API answer 500 or 503?
a: 503 Service Unavailable, ideally with a retry header, because it tells clients the condition is temporary and a later retry may succeed. A 500 is a generic server error and invites investigation rather than a timed retry. Clients still need backoff so they do not hammer the API when it comes back.

q: A booking API has one endpoint, POST /api, with bodies such as {"action": "getBooking", "id": 5} and {"action": "cancelBooking", "id": 5}. Which RMM level is it, and what changes would take it to level 2?
a: Level 0: HTTP is only a transport for RPC-style messages, so there are no resources and no HTTP semantics. Level 1 gives each booking its own URI, /bookings/5. Level 2 then uses the verbs and status codes properly: GET /bookings/5 to read (200 or 404) and DELETE /bookings/5, or a PATCH of its status, to cancel (204).

q: An API exposes GET /v1/rooms/{room-id} to read a room and GET /v1/rooms/{room-id}/book to make a booking. The team says it is level 2 because it has resources. Do you agree?
a: No. It has resource URIs, which is level 1, but it uses GET for a state-changing action and puts a verb in the path, so it does not use HTTP verbs as level 2 requires. GET must be safe: caches, crawlers or retries could create bookings by accident. Model bookings as a resource: POST /v1/rooms/{room-id}/bookings returning 201 with the new booking's location.

q: A mobile client hard-codes 40 URL patterns and breaks whenever the server reorganises its URLs. Which RMM level addresses this, and what does it demand of the client?
a: Level 3, HATEOAS: responses carry hypermedia links to related resources and next actions, so the server controls URL structure and the client discovers it from responses. That loosens coupling and lets the API evolve. The client must be written to follow links instead of building URLs, and responses get somewhat larger.

q: A teammate says moving the API from RMM level 2 to level 3 will raise its throughput under load. Do you agree?
a: Not as stated. RMM grades how fully an API uses resources, HTTP semantics and hypermedia. The lecture links higher levels with scalability and evolvability through looser coupling and cacheable, uniform interfaces, but adding links does not by itself make requests faster. Throughput has to be shown with load tests.

q: A mobile screen needs a customer, their last five orders and the product names, which now takes three REST calls over slow networks. Separately, a public product catalogue is read millions of times a day through HTTP caches. Would you use GraphQL for both?
a: Use GraphQL for the mobile screen: one query to one endpoint returns exactly those fields and avoids over- and under-fetching across three calls. Keep REST for the catalogue, because resource URLs and standard HTTP caching serve repeated identical reads cheaply, while GraphQL queries are hard to cache in web caches. The cost is running two styles, which is justified by two different access patterns.

q: A team implements 'place order' as a GraphQL query because the call returns the new order. Critique this.
a: Placing an order changes data, so it should be a mutation; queries are for reading. Making it a query misleads clients and tools that treat queries as safe to repeat or cache, and an automatic retry could place a second order. Subscriptions are the third operation type, for pushing updates as they happen, such as order status changes.

q: Team A writes the API code first and generates documentation afterwards. Team B agrees an OpenAPI description with consumers before writing code. What does B's design-first approach buy, and what does it cost?
a: It separates the interface from the backend implementation, so consumers can review and build against the contract early, and the documentation matches the API from the start. OpenAPI is a vendor-neutral standard format, so tools and consumers on any stack can use it. The cost is upfront agreement time, and the contract must then be kept in sync with the code.

q: Your API is at version 2.4.1. Give the new version for each change: (a) an optional 'notes' field is added to the order response; (b) 'amount' is renamed to 'total'; (c) a rounding bug is fixed without changing the contract.
a: (a) 2.5.0: a backward-compatible feature bumps the minor version. (b) 3.0.0: renaming a field breaks existing consumers, so the major version goes up. (c) 2.4.2: a backward-compatible fix bumps the patch. Change (b) also needs version 2 kept available for a while, because the rules say not to take anything away abruptly.

q: An API puts its full version in every URI, such as /v1.1/orders, and changes the URI for every minor release, so all consumers must update their URLs each time. Propose a better strategy.
a: Version for breaking changes only. Put just the major version in the URI (/v1/orders) or move it to an Accept or custom header, and make minor and patch releases backward compatible so the URIs consumers call stay the same. Keep the old major version running with an explicit service level while consumers migrate. URI versioning is visible and easy to test; header versioning keeps URIs stable but is harder to see and to try in a browser.

q: A field is deprecated and only 3% of calls still use it. The team wants to delete it next week. What do the versioning rules say?
a: Don't take anything away abruptly. Removal is a breaking change, so it belongs in a new major version, while the current version keeps the field under an explicit service level and the change is announced through the developer portal. The 3% may include an important partner, so check who they are before setting the deadline.

q: Each of 12 services currently implements its own token validation, rate limits and request validation, each slightly differently. What would you propose, and what must stay in the services?
a: Put an API gateway in front as the single gatekeeper, so authentication, rate limits and schema validation are enforced consistently for every client. Each service must still authorise business actions, because a valid token does not prove permission on a particular resource, and must validate the data it relies on. The gateway becomes a critical component and must be highly available.

q: An activity feed receives new items every second and pages with ?page=N&limit=50. Users scrolling down see duplicate items. Diagnose the problem and fix it.
a: Offset pagination drifts: new items inserted at the top push earlier items onto the next page. Use cursor pagination, asking for items after the last one seen, with a stable sort order and a unique tie-breaker, since a timestamp alone can skip or repeat items with equal times. The cost is that clients can no longer jump straight to page 37.

q: A client retries every failed call to a slow partner API five times immediately. During a partner outage, the partner receives six times its normal traffic and the client's threads are exhausted. What would you change?
a: Add a timeout so calls cannot wait indefinitely, retry with exponential backoff, and put a circuit breaker in front of the partner that stops calling it after repeated failures and returns a fallback. Bulkhead isolation keeps the partner's calls from using up threads needed for other work. The trade-off is that users get degraded responses during the outage instead of eventual success.

q: An operations lead proposes CPU usage as the main health metric for a public API. Does it show what users experience?
a: No. CPU is an infrastructure metric, and an API can fail requests or respond slowly while CPU is low, for example while waiting on a dependency. Users experience latency, failure rate and uptime, so track application metrics (requests per minute, latency, failure rate) alongside infrastructure ones (uptime, memory and CPU). CPU is still useful for capacity planning.

q: A tester checks performance by repeatedly sending requests from a manual API client on a laptop, then reports that the API 'handles load fine'. The target is 3 seconds for 90% of requests at 5,000 concurrent users. Do you accept the result?
a: No. Manual requests from one laptop produce neither the target concurrency nor repeatable conditions, so results vary with the laptop and network and say little about the 90th percentile. Run automated load and stress tests that generate the defined concurrency and duration from a controlled environment, and report percentile latency against the target. Stress tests then show where the API breaks beyond that load.

q: An API passes all its functional tests and will be public from launch. What else would you check before production?
a: Security: deny by default, least privilege, rejecting illegal input, HTTPS only, correct role permissions, no internal data leaking into public responses, and rate limiting. Performance: load and stress tests against the expected traffic. Usability for developers, and monitoring in place for latency and failure rate. Functional tests show that the contract works, not that the API is safe or fast enough.

q: Average responses are 2 KB of JSON, one report endpoint returns 3 MB of JSON, and the API also serves images. Where would you enable gzip?
a: Enable it for the large JSON report and other big text responses, where the bandwidth saved outweighs the compression CPU. Skip it for small payloads, where the cost is not worth it, and for already-compressed content such as images. Measure response size and latency before and after, rather than turning it on everywhere.

q: A mobile list screen downloads full 40-field product objects to display three fields, and an edit screen sends the whole object with PUT to change one price. What would you change in each?
a: For the list, use a partial response so the server returns only the requested fields, which cuts payload and parsing time. For the edit, use PATCH with only the fields to modify, plus any enclosing parent objects. The two are different tools: a partial response trims what the server sends, and PATCH trims what the client sends.

q: Match each need to OAuth, JWT or SAML: (a) a third-party budgeting app needs delegated access to a user's bank transactions; (b) staff already signed in to the corporate portal should reach a partner web app without logging in again; (c) the access token should carry the issuer, subject and expiry in a compact form.
a: (a) OAuth, the authorisation framework through which the client obtains an access token from an authorisation server. (b) SAML, a single sign-on standard that passes identity from an existing session using an XML document. (c) JWT, a token format that can be used inside OAuth. A design note saying 'JWT instead of OAuth' confuses a token format with the framework for obtaining tokens.

q: A browser web app gets a CORS error calling your API, but the same request works from a command-line client. What do you check?
a: Check that the server's CORS policy allows the app's origin, scheme, port, methods, headers and credentials, and that the server can answer the pre-flight request without error. Then check that the API gateway relays the pre-flight response to the browser. The command-line client works because CORS is enforced only by browsers.

q: A teammate proposes a strict CORS policy as the main protection for a payment API. Is that enough?
a: No. CORS only controls whether a browser lets a page from another origin read the response. Scripts, servers and other non-browser clients ignore it entirely. The API must still authenticate and authorise each call, validate payloads, and apply rate limits.

q: Your API receives a million requests a day, 30% of them with missing or null fields, and the application crashes on the nulls. How do you handle this in production?
a: Validate requests against the API schema at the edge, checking content, parameters and headers, and reject bad ones with a 400 that explains which field is wrong. Inside the service, handle optional fields defensively so one bad request cannot crash the process. Log and monitor the rejection rate, because 30% suggests a client bug or a confusing contract worth fixing at the source.

q: An Order service and an Inventory service have separate databases. At peak there are 2,000 orders a minute, and Inventory is sometimes slow. Would you use two-phase commit or a saga?
a: A saga. Two-phase commit holds locks across both services until both are ready, so a slow Inventory stalls every order and couples their availability. In a saga each service commits locally and publishes an event, and a failure triggers compensation such as cancelling the order. You accept eventual consistency and must design compensations and idempotent handlers.

q: In the lecture's centrally directed saga, Inventory replies 'Failed to Reserve Items'. What happens next, and why is this orchestration even though messages go through an event bus?
a: The coordinator sends a compensating 'Delete Order' to undo the order already committed and notifies the user. It is orchestration because one coordinator decides the next step; an event bus is only the transport. In choreography, each service would react to the failure event on its own.

q: A mobile app calls six microservices directly, each with its own address, authentication scheme and response format. What problems does this cause, and what does an API gateway fix?
a: The app is coupled to each service's location and contract, makes many round trips, and has to handle six security schemes, so every internal change risks breaking a released app. A gateway gives one entry point with central security and routing, can compose several calls into one response, and lets services move or split behind it. It adds a hop and a component that must be highly available.

q: A clinic platform's first two APIs are designed as follows. API 1: URI /v2.3/appointments/{patient-id}/book, service BookingManager, input the patient id, output the list of all doctors, HTTP verb GET. API 2: URI /v2.3/appointments/{patient-id}/cancel, service BookingManager, inputs the patient id and patient name, output the list of all patients' appointments, HTTP verb GET. (1) Do they comply with RMM level 2? (2) Propose a versioning strategy that affects consumers less. (3) Give corrected interfaces.
a: (1) No. They have resource-like URIs, which is level 1, but use GET for state-changing actions and put verbs in the path, so the HTTP verbs are not used as level 2 requires; GET must be safe. (2) Use semantic versioning, with only the major version in the URI (/v2) or in a header, and keep minor and patch releases backward compatible so consumers are unaffected by them. (3) Book: POST /v2/patients/{patient-id}/appointments with the doctor id and time slot as inputs, returning 201 and the created appointment with its location. Cancel: DELETE /v2/patients/{patient-id}/appointments/{appointment-id}, or PATCH its status to cancelled, returning 204 or the updated appointment. Drop the redundant patient name and the unrelated lists of all doctors or all appointments.

q: Design a RESTful API for a cleaning-service platform. Customers make one-off orders or subscribe to OnceAFortnight, OnceAWeek or TwiceAWeek plans, change or cancel subscriptions, and pay; the mobile app retries on timeouts. Give resources, verbs and status codes, and explain how you handle retries.
a: Resources: /customers/{customer-id}/orders (POST creates a one-off order, 201; GET lists orders with ?status= and pagination), /plans (GET), and /customers/{customer-id}/subscriptions (POST subscribes, 201; PATCH /subscriptions/{subscription-id} changes the plan, 200 or 204; DELETE cancels, 204), plus /payments (POST, 201). Use plural kebab-case nouns, no verbs, path variables for identity and query parameters for filtering. Retried POSTs to orders, subscriptions and payments carry an idempotency key, and the server returns the recorded outcome for a repeat. Aim for level 2, and add links (level 3) such as a subscription's cancel and change-plan links if clients would benefit; version as /v1.

q: A published API at version 1 has 200 partner integrations. You must split 'name' into 'firstName' and 'lastName', add an optional loyalty-points field, and fix a currency-rounding bug. Plan the releases and the partner impact.
a: Ship the bug fix as a patch and the optional loyalty field as a minor release; neither breaks partners, so they need no changes. The name split changes meaning and removes a field, so it goes into version 2 (/v2 or a v2 media type), while version 1 keeps returning 'name' under an explicit service level. Announce the change and its timeline through the developer portal, and track v1 usage per partner before retiring it. The cost is running two versions side by side for the migration period.

q: A public payment API serves a browser single-page app and partner servers. It receives a million requests a day, 30% with malformed or null fields, and retried POSTs have caused some duplicate charges. Design its security and robustness, and name one drawback of your design.
a: Put a gateway in front for TLS, OAuth 2.0 access tokens (JWT is one possible format), per-client rate limits and quotas, and schema validation that rejects malformed requests with a 400. Services still authorise each action and validate business invariants. Configure CORS for the single-page app's origin only, remembering that CORS is not authentication. Require an idempotency key on payment POSTs so retries return the original result, and add timeouts, circuit breakers on downstream calls, and monitoring of latency and failure rate. Drawback: the gateway is a critical shared component, and strict validation will initially reject many partner requests until partners fix their clients.

q: After a release, the 95th-percentile latency of GET /orders rose from 300 ms to 4 seconds, while database query times are unchanged. Give the most likely causes, how you would confirm them, a fix, and the fix's drawback.
a: Fast queries mean the time is spent elsewhere: a new or slower downstream call, a thread or connection pool being exhausted, or larger payloads from the release. Confirm with distributed traces to find the slow span, then check pool metrics and the release diff. If a downstream call is the cause, add a timeout and circuit breaker with a fallback, or call it in parallel or cache the result. The drawback is degraded or slightly stale responses when the fallback or cache is used, so the change needs a load test before release.

q: A product team must choose between REST and GraphQL for a mobile dashboard that aggregates data from six microservices; a public catalogue endpoint on the same platform is mostly anonymous, repeated reads. Recommend a style for each and give the trade-offs.
a: GraphQL for the dashboard: it is client-driven, so one query to one endpoint fetches exactly the fields needed from several services, cutting mobile round trips and over-fetching, and the schema and type system document the data. REST for the catalogue: it is server-driven and resource-oriented, and identical repeated reads benefit from ordinary HTTP and CDN caching, which GraphQL makes hard. The cost is two styles to run and secure, plus resolvers that must call the six services efficiently.

q: A team splits a monolith by turning each in-process method call into a remote call one for one. A single page now makes 40 remote calls and is slow. Diagnose the problem.
a: Remote calls cost far more than in-process calls, so remote APIs need to be coarser-grained than the library-style interfaces they replaced. The services should expose fewer, larger operations around business capabilities, which may mean revisiting the boundaries. Moving responsibilities between services later is harder once they sit across process boundaries, so the split deserves care up front.

q: Order and Inventory now own separate databases. A manager asks for 'one ACID transaction across both, like before'. How do you respond?
a: Microservices favour decentralised data, where each service manages its own database and coordinates with others without a shared transaction. That means eventual consistency plus compensating operations, such as releasing stock if the order fails. If the business truly needs both changes to commit atomically, that suggests the data belongs in one service rather than a distributed transaction.

q: A company has separate UI, backend and database teams, and every new feature becomes a cross-team project needing budget approval. What does Conway's law predict about its system, and what would you change?
a: The system will mirror those silos: layers owned by different teams, tangled together, with logic pushed into whichever part a team can touch. Organise cross-functional teams around business capabilities, each with the full range of skills from user experience to database, so each team's service matches a capability. Teams then own their service end to end, including running it.

q: An architect proposes putting routing, message transformation and business rules into a central message bus so the services can stay simple. Critique the proposal.
a: That is the enterprise-service-bus style, with smarts in the pipe. Microservices prefer smart endpoints and dumb pipes: the logic stays in cohesive services and the bus only routes messages. A smart central bus couples every service to one shared component and its team, so changes queue up there. The cost of the microservice style is that each service owns more of its own logic.

q: Your small Shipping team must integrate with a large, established ERP whose team will not change anything for you. Should Shipping be a Conformist or build an Anticorruption Layer?
a: It depends on whether Shipping's model can live with the ERP's. If it can, and the team cannot sustain the effort of translating, conform: it is cheaper. If the ERP is a Big Ball of Mud that would distort Shipping's model, build an Anticorruption Layer that translates to Shipping's ubiquitous language, accepting the cost of maintaining the translation.

q: Eight downstream contexts each maintain their own translation of the Customer context's model, and every Customer change breaks several of them. What should the Customer team offer instead?
a: An Open Host Service, a protocol or set of services giving access to the context, with a Published Language such as a documented JSON Schema. Downstream teams can then consume and translate easily, and an anticorruption layer becomes less crucial for them. The Customer team takes on keeping that public interface stable and versioned.

q: Marketing wants a small piece of Billing's data, but Billing's model does not really provide what Marketing needs, and integrating would take months. What mapping fits?
a: Separate Ways: integration would not give a significant payoff because the functionality sought is not fully provided by the source ubiquitous language. Marketing builds its own specialised solution. The cost is some duplicated capability, which is cheaper than months of integration.

q: Two teams propose a shared kernel of 40 classes so they can stop translating between their contexts. What concerns would you raise?
a: A shared kernel should be a small common model, and even then it is hard to conceive and maintain, because it needs open communication and constant agreement between both teams. Forty classes would bind their release schedules together. A Customer-Supplier relationship, or an Open Host Service with a Published Language, keeps the teams more independent.

q: When an order is placed, the Loyalty context must add points. Loyalty is offline for 20 minutes every night for maintenance. Would you integrate with REST or messaging?
a: Messaging. Order publishes a domain event and Loyalty processes it when it comes back, which removes the temporal coupling of a blocking REST call that would fail or stall orders during the outage. It needs at-least-once delivery and an idempotent receiver in Loyalty. The trade-off is that points appear later rather than immediately.

q: After a broker redelivery, the Loyalty subscriber processes the same OrderPlaced event twice and awards double points. What is the fix?
a: At-least-once delivery means redelivery is expected, so the receiver must be idempotent. Record processed event IDs and skip duplicates, or make the update safe to reapply, such as 'set points for order X' instead of 'add points'. Switching off redelivery would just swap duplicates for lost messages.

q: To save time, the Reporting context reads the Order context's tables directly. What is wrong with this?
a: Database integration is the type to avoid. It couples Reporting to Order's internal storage, breaks the bounded context's encapsulation, and means any change to Order's schema can break Reporting without warning. Use Order's published API, or subscribe to its domain events and build Reporting's own read model, at the cost of some lag.

q: A team chose SOAP RPC between two contexts because the call looks just like a local procedure call. What risks does that hide, and what practices reduce them?
a: The call still crosses the network, so it lacks robustness against latency, network failure and upstream failure, and it couples the client strongly to the service and protocol. The lecture's practices are an Open Host Service with a Published Language upstream and an Anticorruption Layer downstream. If the flow does not need an immediate answer, messaging would remove the temporal coupling.

q: A Sprint aggregate holds direct object references to all its BacklogItems, which hold all their Tasks. Loading a sprint takes three seconds and concurrent edits often fail. What would you change?
a: Design small aggregates and reference other aggregates by identity. Make BacklogItem its own aggregate that holds a SprintId value object, and have Sprint hold BacklogItemIds rather than objects. Smaller aggregates load faster, use less memory and succeed more often under concurrency. Changes that span both are then made through domain events in separate transactions, which means eventual consistency.

q: The business says that when a backlog item is committed, the sprint's capacity must never be exceeded, checked at the same commit. Today Sprint and BacklogItem are separate aggregates updated by a domain event. What do you do?
a: This invariant must hold within one transaction, and the delay of a domain event would allow unacceptable inconsistency. So consider merging the commitment data into one aggregate within the same bounded context, which the lecture advises when two must be updated immediately one after the other. The cost is a larger aggregate with more contention, so first check whether the business could accept detecting and correcting an over-commit instead.

q: In code review, the Order aggregate has only getters and setters, while an OrderService checks that the total does not exceed the credit limit and then sets the status. What is the problem?
a: It is an anaemic domain model: business logic has leaked out of the aggregate into an application service. Other code paths can set the status without checking the rule, so the invariant is not protected inside the boundary. Move the rule into a method on Order, such as place(), that enforces it before changing state.

q: A team models Money as an entity with its own ID and table, and Customer as a value object. Critique the model.
a: It is backwards. Money is a value object: it has no identity of its own, is immutable, and describes an amount. Customer is an entity with a unique identity whose attributes change over time. Making Money an entity adds needless IDs and invites shared mutable amounts, while making Customer a value object makes it impossible to track one customer across changes.

q: A service commits an Order and then publishes OrderPlaced as a separate step. Occasionally the process crashes between the two. What is the consequence, and what is the fix?
a: The order exists but the event is lost, so subscribers such as Inventory and Billing never learn about it and stay stale. Commit the modified aggregate and the domain event in the same transaction, then deliver recorded events reliably afterwards, including after recovery. Subscribers still need to be idempotent, because that delivery can repeat.

q: Shipping receives OrderPlaced events carrying only the orderId and calls the Order API back for the address and tenantId on every event. The Order API is now overloaded. What would you change?
a: Make the event carry all the properties of the command that caused it, and enrich it with extra data such as tenantId and the delivery address, so consumers need not query the publisher. That removes the remote calls and decouples Shipping from Order's availability. The cost is larger events and an event schema that must be kept stable for every consumer.

q: On a forum, replies sometimes appear on other users' screens before the post they answer. Which property is violated, and what must the design guarantee?
a: Causal consistency: causally related operations must be seen in the same order by every dependent node. A reply depends on its post, so its event must never be applied before the post's event.
